cards.25.who: Security/AI, PM, CEO. Source: the "mass audience" focus in the brand JD; a product test for everyday users. Scored on: communication, simplifying without being wrong.
cards.25.understand: This is a test of **copywriting + judgement**. The best answer: a simple metaphor in Vietnamese, **say it only when needed**, and **don't over-promise**. Bonus: say the sentence in Vietnamese to show you understand local users.
cards.25.answer_label: Sample answer (EN, with one sentence in Vietnamese).
cards.25.answer:
**"I wouldn't explain it unless she asks. I'd show it at the moment it matters, in one sentence she already understands."**

The sentence, in Vietnamese, would be something like: "Tin nhắn của bạn được khóa lại. Chỉ bạn và người nhận mở được, kể cả chúng tôi cũng không đọc được." Your message is locked; only you and the person you're sending to can open it; not even we can read it.

The metaphor is a sealed envelope, not a lock icon. Lock icons are everywhere and mean nothing.

Two cautions. Don't over-promise: encryption doesn't stop someone screenshotting, and it doesn't stop a scammer she's chosen to talk to. So the copy says what it protects and stops there. And repeat it at the moments that matter: the first chat, linking a new device, backing up history. Not on every screen.

I'd test the sentence with five people over sixty, ideally my own relatives first, and check they can say it back in their own words.
cards.25.why: It flips the question ("don't explain, show it at the right moment"), has a real Vietnamese sentence, warns against over-promising (a sign of someone who understands security), and ends with a way to check it.
cards.25.five: A natural Vietnamese sentence, a warning not to over-promise, and "I tried this on my mum" is true.
cards.25.evidence: ✅ Knowledge from Section 9.2. 🟦 Try the Vietnamese sentence with your parents or older people before the interview, so you can say *"I tried this on my mum last week."*
cards.25.hook: **"A sealed envelope, not a lock."** Show · One sentence · Don't over-promise · Key moments · Test with 5.

cards.25.must: (1) don't explain unless needed; (2) the Vietnamese sentence; (3) don't over-promise (screenshots, scammers); (4) test with older people.
cards.25.drill: Say the Vietnamese sentence naturally 5 times.
cards.25.traps: Explaining public and private keys. Putting a green lock everywhere. Promising "100% secure".

cards.27.who: Security/AI, PM, HM, CEO. Source: the scam situation in Vietnam (Section 2), "AI-powered secure communication" in the brand JD. This may be their **central product problem**. Scored on: understanding warnings, psychology and measurement.
cards.27.understand: Research on security warnings (for example studies of browser SSL warnings, Akhawe & Felt 2013; "habituation" when people see the same warning again and again) shows this: users ignore warnings when they appear too often and look the same. You don't need to cite names, but using the right ideas, **habituation** and **warning budget**, will make a strong impression on Hằng.
cards.27.answer:
**"Treat warnings like a budget. Every false alarm spends trust we need for the real one."**

Four design moves.

One, tiers. Most of the time, nothing. Low-risk context, a quiet note: "You haven't chatted with this person before." High risk, a clear interruption: a new contact, a link, and a request for money or an OTP in the same thread. Only that last tier ever looks alarming.

Two, specific, not generic. "This message asks for an OTP. Banks never ask for OTPs in chat" beats "This message may be suspicious." Specific warnings get read; generic ones get habituated.

Three, vary and place it at the moment of action. A warning at the moment you tap the link or type an OTP is far stronger than one at the top of the chat, and changing the design for the highest tier fights habituation.

Four, an easy right action. Block and report in one tap, and a way to ask a trusted contact, "Hỏi người thân", because in Vietnam a lot of scam defence is a family member saying "don't".

And I'd measure it like CYBERhythm: not how many warnings we show, but how many led to a block or report, and how many were dismissed and later reported as scams.
cards.27.why: The ideas of "warning budget" and "habituation" show research depth. The OTP example fits Vietnam. "Hỏi người thân" (ask a family member) is a purely local idea (G-local). Measurement links back to your real CYBERhythm experience.
cards.27.five: Warning budget, habituation, one concrete OTP example, "Hỏi người thân", and measuring by outcomes, not by counting warnings. Holds up under the 10% false positive question.
cards.27.evidence: ✅ CYBERhythm triage. ✅ Section 9.2. 🟨 "Hỏi người thân" is your own new idea, not a feature that exists anywhere yet; present it as a proposal.
cards.27.hook: **"Warning budget."** 4 moves: Tiers · Specific · At the moment · Right action (+ ask a family member). "T-S-M-R: Tôi Sợ Mất Rồi" (I'm afraid it's gone).
